pages.name: Up 2
pages.text: This is the square from lesson 3, `f(x) = x²`. `f(x) + 2` adds 2 to every output, so every point rises 2 and the whole graph slides up 2, a [[vertical shift]]. Drag it up or down.

pages.alt: A graph of y equals f(x) plus 2 equals x squared plus 2 on a grid of whole squares, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. A marked point reads (2, 4) goes to (2, 6).

pages.name: Down 3
pages.task: Slide `y = x²` to make `y = x² − 3`. Where does the point `(1, 1)` land?
pages.why: `x² − 3` puts 1 through the square to get 1, then takes 3 off, giving −2. The input stays 1, so `(1, 1)` drops straight down to `(1, −2)`.

pages.name: The transmitter
pages.text: The transmitter's rule from lesson 2, `S(p) = 0.16p + 4`, is the line `0.16p` slid up 4 mA. At 50% that line gives 8 mA, so the transmitter sends 12 mA. Sliding changes no steepness, so the slope stays 0.16 mA per percent.
pages.alt: A graph of S(p) equals 0.16p plus 4 on a grid of whole squares, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. A marked point reads (50 percent, 8 mA) goes to (50 percent, 12 mA).

pages.name: Which way?
pages.task: Now make `y = (x − 3)²`. Which way will the graph slide?
pages.why: `(x − 3)²` takes 3 off the input before squaring, so it gives 0 only at `x = 3`, where `(3 − 3)² = 0`. The bottom moves from 0 to 3, to the right.

pages.name: Right 3
pages.text: `f(x − 3)` takes 3 off the input first, so each input must be 3 bigger to give the old output. Now 3, 4 and 5 give 0, 1 and 4, and `(2, 4)` moves to `(5, 4)`. This slide along the `x`-axis is a [[horizontal shift]].
pages.alt: A graph of y equals f(x minus 3) equals (x minus 3) squared on a grid of whole squares, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. A marked point reads (2, 4) goes to (5, 4).

pages.name: A plus inside
pages.why: `(x + 2)²` adds 2 to the input first, so it gives 0 at `x = −2`, where `(−2 + 2)² = 0`. Each input can be 2 smaller, so the bottom slides 2 to the left.

pages.name: Left 2
pages.text: `f(x + 2)` adds 2 to the input first, so each input can be 2 smaller. Now −2, −1 and 0 give 0, 1 and 4, and `(2, 4)` moves to `(0, 4)`. The bracket is 0 at `x = −2`, so the bottom sits there.

pages.name: The root
pages.why: A root can only start where its inside is 0, and `x − 4` is 0 at `x = 4`. The whole graph, starting dot and all, slides 4 to the right.

pages.name: Both at once
pages.text: The two moves do not get in each other's way. `(x − 3)² + 2` slides right 3 and up 2, so the bottom goes from `(0, 0)` to `(3, 2)` and `(2, 4)` goes to `(5, 6)`. Drag it anywhere.

pages.alt: A graph of y equals f(x minus 3) plus 2 equals (x minus 3) squared plus 2 on a grid of whole squares, input along the bottom and output up the side. A dashed copy shows where it started. A marked point reads (2, 4) goes to (5, 6).

pages.name: Two moves
pages.why: Inside, `x + 1` is 0 at `x = −1`, so the graph slides 1 to the left. Outside, the − 4 slides it down 4, so the bottom `(0, 0)` lands on `(−1, −4)`.

pages.name: Name the rule
pages.task: The cube `y = x³` has slid, so its middle point `(0, 0)` sits at `(2, −1)`. Which rule is it?
pages.why: The middle point moved right 2 and down 1, so the rule is `f(x − 2) − 1 = (x − 2)³ − 1`. Check one point. At `x = 3`, `(3 − 2)³ − 1 = 1 − 1 = 0`, and the graph passes through `(3, 0)`.

pages.name: A reading 1 mA high
pages.task: A transmitter sends 1 mA too much, so it sends `S(p) + 1`. What does it send at 50%?
pages.why: `S(50) = 0.16 × 50 + 4 = 12` mA, and the error adds 1 outside, so it sends 13 mA. The whole line slides up 1 mA and keeps its slope.
